queue.tree_name: The Southern Mahogany of Edinburgh Gardens
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the rough fibrous bark held on the trunk where the park's river red gum is smooth and pale, on a trunk 4.34 metres round and 25 metres tall. It stands off Alfred Crescent in Edinburgh Gardens.
queue.story:
This is a beach tree living in Fitzroy North. Eucalyptus botryoides belongs to the sandy, salt-touched country of the south-east Australian coast, behind dunes and around swamp margins, and it does not turn up this far inland on its own. Somebody carried it here and planted it, in a park laid out from 1862 whose heritage citation notes the number of mature specimen trees put in from that period onward. Which of those plantings this one belongs to is written down nowhere we can find.

queue.tree_name: The Finer Holm Oak of Edinburgh Gardens
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, about 5.56 metres round, the thickest on this page, crowded close by nearby elms. It stands near the bowling club in Edinburgh Gardens, Fitzroy North.
queue.story: Edinburgh Gardens has two holm oaks, and the National Trust of Australia has a view about which one to look at. Its Significant Tree Register calls this the finer of the two examples of the species in the gardens, and it is certainly the heavier: the City of Yarra records 177 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which is about 5.56 metres of girth, since that 177 is a width across the trunk and not a measurement around it. That is the thickest trunk here and a record nowhere else: the Trust's own significance statement points to a tree at Talindert, near Camperdown in western Victoria, as the biggest of its kind in Victoria.
